The calculations are based on higher-order finite differences and are performed on refined spatial and temporal meshes to resolve all the important energy-carrying scales.
The near-field large-scale structures include the shear layer vortices, the counter-rotating vortex pair (CVP), the horseshoe vortex system, and wake and wall vortices.
The dynamics of these structures are significantly influenced by a time-periodic interaction between the jet hole boundary layer and the approaching crossflow.
The periodic behavior has a Strouhal number of 0.44 based on the jet velocity and diameter.
A new mechanism for the formation of shear layer vortices is identified, involving alternate shedding of positive and negative vorticity.
The predicted turbulent statistics show reasonable agreement with experimental measurements.
The film cooling configuration differs from single-jet-in-crossflow studies in the spanwise boundary conditions and lower blowing ratios, leading to a non-uniform jet-exit profile.
Inclusion of the flow development within the coolant hole is important for accurately specifying the jet-exit conditions and their influence on the downstream flow structures.
Direct numerical simulation (DNS) allows resolving all the energy-carrying scales without the need for turbulence models, but poses significant computational challenges.
The jet-to-crossflow velocity ratio studied in this work is 0.5.
The computational work was performed on a variety of high-performance computing platforms, including Cray C-90, Cray YMP, NAVO T3E, and NAVO T-90 computers.
The primary contributors to this work include graduate students Frank Muldoon, Mayank Tyagi, Asif Hoda, Chirdeep Sharma, and research associate Dr. M. Taeibi-Rahni.

The computational codes developed for this research include a dual-time stepping pseudo-compressibility based approach, a fractional step approach with a pressure-Poisson solver, and a staggered finite volume code for RANS simulations.
